_note: Milling of the staple grains into flour, which households eat, and bran, which animals eat. Each recipe takes one grain and the shaft work to grind and sift it; the grain itself is grown (wheat_kg, millet_kg, maize_kg). Maize is ground on a metate in practice; the shaft work and yield are the same order, so one recipe shape serves all three. Bran is a joint output with no reference price, a recorded waste (data/world/waste_heaps.json), fed to draught animals and herds (Complaints/544).

flour_kg.basis: per 1000 kg of sifted flour ground between stones from wheat, with the bran sifted out
flour_kg.yield_basis: MILLED AND SIFTED. Stones crack and grind the grain; the flour is bolted through a sieve and the husk and germ that stay on it are bran. Of 1190 kg of grain in, 1000 kg of flour (an extraction of about 84 percent, in the range of 75 to 85 percent usual for stone-milled bolted flour; recalled from milling handbooks, not opened, conf D), 150 kg of bran (about 12.6 percent, conf D) and 40 kg lost as moisture and dust (about 3.4 percent, the few percent the whole-meal entry this replaces took as its loss; conf C, author's estimate). Shaft work: grinding grain between stones takes on the order of a tenth of a megajoule per kilogram of grain (author's estimate from the output of a hand quern at the 75 W a person sustains, about a kilogram an hour, and of water mills; not checked against a primary source offline, conf C), scaled to the grain ground. The shaft work is priced through the energy market, so whoever supplies it (people at a quern or treadmill, or a water wheel and the millwrights who build and tend it) is paid there. Labour is feeding the hopper, dressing the stones, bolting and sacking, a few hours a tonne (conf D). Millstone wear is not charged. The bran carries no share of the cost (a recorded waste with no reference price); it is the winter supplement of herds and draught animals (95_herds.json, 94_agri_organics_gaps.json).

flour_kg_wholemeal.basis: per 1000 kg of whole-meal flour ground between stones, from wheat; the bran stays in, beside the sifted recipe that parts flour from bran
flour_kg_wholemeal.yield_basis: MILLED. Stones crack and grind the whole grain and nothing is sifted out: the few percent that leaves as moisture and dust is the difference between grain in and flour out (1040 in, 1000 out, conf C). Shaft work: grinding grain between stones takes on the order of a tenth of a megajoule per kilogram (author's estimate from the output of a hand quern at the 75 W a person sustains, about a kilogram an hour, and of water mills, a kilogram per few tens of kilojoules at the wheel; not checked against a primary source offline, conf C). The shaft work is priced through the energy market, so whoever supplies it (people at a quern or treadmill, or a water wheel and the millwrights who build and tend it) is paid there. Labour here is only feeding the hopper, dressing the stones and sacking, a few hours a tonne (conf D). Millstone wear is not charged.

flour_kg_millet_wholemeal.basis: per 1000 kg of whole-meal flour ground between stones, from millet; the bran stays in, beside the sifted recipe that parts flour from bran
flour_kg_millet_wholemeal.yield_basis: MILLED, as flour_kg from wheat: millet is a small hard grain, ground whole; the same mass loss and shaft work are taken (conf C, author's estimate; no separate figure found offline). Labour feeds the hopper and sacks the flour (conf D).

flour_kg_maize_wholemeal.basis: per 1000 kg of whole-meal flour ground between stones, from maize; the bran stays in, beside the sifted recipe that parts flour from bran
flour_kg_maize_wholemeal.yield_basis: MILLED, as flour_kg from wheat: dry maize is ground whole (on a metate in the Americas, a stone mill elsewhere); the same mass loss and shaft work are taken (conf C, author's estimate; no separate figure found offline). Labour feeds the stone and sacks the flour (conf D).
